parts.text:
The point $P$ lies on the curve with equation $y = \ln\left(\frac{1}{3}x\right)$. The $x$-coordinate of $P$ is 3.
Find an equation of the normal to the curve at the point $P$ in the form $y = ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x}$ accept $\frac{3}{3x}$ M1 A1
At $x=3$, $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow m' = -3$ Use of $mm'=-1$ M1
$y - \ln 1 = -3(x-3)$ M1
$y = -3x+9$ Accept $y=9-3x$ A1 (5) [5]
[Note: if $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{3x}$ leading to $y=-9x+27$ is a maximum of M1 A0 M1 M1 A0 = 3/5]

questions.stem:
$\mathrm{f}(x) = 12\cos x - 4\sin x$.
Given that $\mathrm{f}(x) = R\cos(x+\alpha)$, where $R \geqslant 0$ and $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 90°$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find the value of $R$ and the value of $\alpha$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $R\cos\alpha=12$, $R\sin\alpha=4$
$R = \sqrt{(12^2+4^2)} = \sqrt{160}$ Accept if just written down, awrt 12.6 M1 A1
$\tan\alpha = \frac{4}{12}, \Rightarrow \alpha \approx 18.43°$ awrt $18.4°$ M1, A1 (4)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence solve the equation
$12\cos x - 4\sin x = 7$
for $0 \leqslant x < 360°$, giving your answers to one decimal place.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\cos(x+\text{their }\alpha) = \frac{7}{\text{their }R}$ $(\approx 0.5534)$ M1
$x + \text{their }\alpha = 56.4°$ awrt $56°$ A1
$=\ldots, 303.6°$ $360° - \text{their principal value}$ M1
$x = 38.0°, 285.2°$ Ignore solutions out of range A1, A1 (5)
If answers given to more than 1 dp, penalise first time then accept awrt above.

parts.label: c(i)
parts.text:
(c) (i) Write down the minimum value of $12\cos x - 4\sin x$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (c)(i) minimum value is $-\sqrt{160}$ ft their $R$ B1ft (1)

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) Find, to 2 decimal places, the smallest positive value of $x$ for which this minimum value occurs.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(ii) $\cos(x+\text{their }\alpha) = -1$ M1
$x \approx 161.57°$ cao A1 (3) [12]

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text:
(i) $\frac{\cos 2x}{\cos x + \sin x} \equiv \cos x - \sin x, \quad x \neq (n-\frac{1}{4})\pi, n \in \mathbb{Z}$,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a)(i) Use of $\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x$ in an attempt to prove the identity. M1
$\frac{\cos 2x}{\cos x+\sin x} = \frac{\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x}{\cos x+\sin x} = \frac{(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)}{\cos x+\sin x} = \cos x-\sin x$ * cso A1 (2)

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) $\frac{1}{2}(\cos 2x - \sin 2x) \equiv \cos^2 x - \cos x \sin x - \frac{1}{2}$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a)(ii) Use of $\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$ in an attempt to prove the identity. M1
Use of $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$ in an attempt to prove the identity. M1
$\frac{1}{2}(\cos 2x-\sin 2x) = \frac{1}{2}(2\cos^2 x-1-2\sin x\cos x) = \cos^2 x-\cos x\sin x-\frac{1}{2}$ * cso A1 (3)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence, or otherwise, show that the equation
$\cos\theta\left(\frac{\cos 2\theta}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$
can be written as
$\sin 2\theta = \cos 2\theta$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\cos\theta(\cos\theta-\sin\theta) = \frac{1}{2}$ Using (a)(i) M1
$\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta\sin\theta-\frac{1}{2}=0$
$\frac{1}{2}(\cos 2\theta-\sin 2\theta)=0$ Using (a)(ii) M1
$\cos 2\theta = \sin 2\theta$ * A1 (3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Solve, for $0 \leqslant \theta < 2\pi$,
$\sin 2\theta = \cos 2\theta$,
giving your answers in terms of $\pi$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $\tan 2\theta = 1$ M1
$2\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}, \left(\frac{5\pi}{4}, \frac{9\pi}{4}, \frac{13\pi}{4}\right)$ any one correct value of $2\theta$ A1
$\theta = \frac{\pi}{8}, \frac{5\pi}{8}, \frac{9\pi}{8}, \frac{13\pi}{8}$ Obtaining at least 2 solutions in range M1
The 4 correct solutions A1 (4) [12]
If decimals $(0.393, 1.963, 3.534, 5.105)$ or degrees $(22.5°, 112.5°, 202.5°, 292.5°)$ are given, but all 4 solutions are found, penalise one A mark only. Ignore solutions out of range.

questions.stem:
The functions f and g are defined by
$\mathrm{f}: x \mapsto 2x + \ln 2, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}$,
$\mathrm{g}: x \mapsto \mathrm{e}^{2x}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Prove that the composite function gf is
$\mathrm{gf}: x \mapsto 4\mathrm{e}^{4x}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\mathrm{gf}(x) = \mathrm{e}^{2(2x+\ln 2)}$ M1
$= \mathrm{e}^{4x}\mathrm{e}^{2\ln 2}$ M1
$= \mathrm{e}^{4x}\mathrm{e}^{\ln 4}$ M1
$= 4\mathrm{e}^{4x}$ Give mark at this point, cso A1 (4)
(Hence $\mathrm{gf}: x \mapsto 4\mathrm{e}^{4x}, x \in \mathbb{R}$)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Sketch the curve with equation $y = \mathrm{gf}(x)$, and show the coordinates of the point where the curve cuts the $y$-axis.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (b) Shape and point B1 (1)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Write down the range of gf.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (c) Range is $\mathbb{R}_+$ Accept $\mathrm{gf}(x) > 0$, $y > 0$ B1 (1)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Find the value of $x$ for which $\frac{d}{dx}[\mathrm{gf}(x)] = 3$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $\frac{d}{dx}[\mathrm{gf}(x)] = 16\mathrm{e}^{4x}$
$\mathrm{e}^{4x} = \frac{3}{16}$ M1 A1
$4x = \ln\frac{3}{16}$ M1
$x \approx -0.418$ A1 (4) [10]
